items.abstract: When indivisible objects, such as heirlooms or tickets to sports events, do not divide evenly among agents with equal claims, some agents must receive more objects than others. Can picking first compensate those with fewer objects? We propose two principles of compensatory fairness. An agent with fewer objects must not envy a larger bundle with any one of its objects removed, and priority advantages among agents with equally many objects must alternate rather than accumulate. Non-wastefulness, neutrality and an object-wise form of Maskin monotonicity characterize the draft rules, in which agents pick in a fixed sequence. Adding the two principles and envy-freeness up to one object singles out the block--snake draft, in which agents with fewer objects pick first in every round and each group's order reverses between rounds. Among draft rules, compensation is compatible with strategy-proofness, but envy-freeness up to one object is not: once at least two agents receive more than one object, no draft that satisfies it is even weakly strategy-proof, and with two such agents the conflict extends to all non-wasteful and neutral rules. items.title: Moral Consumers and the Environment
items.abstract: We study the taxation of environmentally harmful goods when consumers have a Kantian desire to ``do the right thing''. A consumer evaluates her buying strategy, a rule that specifies whether to buy, by the material payoff she would obtain if others followed the same rule with a probability given by her degree of morality. Equilibrium exists and is unique in finite populations with heterogeneous morality. The optimal tax depends crucially on whether consumers are aware that tax revenue is returned to them. If they are, the Pigovian tax is optimal under homogeneous morality, whatever consumers know about environmental costs, and we give conditions under which it remains the unique optimum under heterogeneous morality. If they are not, the optimal tax is lower, and more so the more moral consumers are. Under a quota system such as the EU Emissions Trading System, any cap at least as stringent as the Pigovian quota admits an equilibrium in which morality has no effect on consumers who are aware of the system.

items.abstract: Risk-sharing arrangements such as reinsurance programs and catastrophe pools must satisfy operational constraints, including capacity limits, attachment bands, retention rules and cession limits. Under distortion risk measures, the unconstrained optimum assigns each loss layer to the participant for whom that layer is least costly, but operational constraints break this layerwise rule, and there is no general method to compute the constrained optimum. We show that, for comonotonic allocations, the participants' distortion risk measures and the operational constraints are linear in the amount of each loss layer held by each participant, so the constrained risk-sharing problem on a discretized loss is a linear program that standard software can solve. Its dual gives supporting prices for the loss layers and the marginal value of relaxing each operational constraint. Where the set of binding constraints changes, the constrained optimal value can have a kink, and the smallest and largest optimal multipliers then give the one-sided effects of relaxing and tightening a constraint. items.abstract: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. items.title: Sanctions, Evasion, and Deterrence: Evidence from Speeding Enforcement
items.abstract: The design of sanctions plays a central role in shaping reoffending behavior. We study the effects of fixed monetary fines and accumulating penalty points on speeding recidivism and liability transfer. Exploiting a large increase in sanctions in Queensland, Australia, we estimate the causal effects of these sanctions on subsequent offending and nomination of other drivers. Higher demerit points increase fine renomination, consistent with strategic blame shifting. Estimated reductions in reoffending are small among offenders facing higher fines alone. Reoffending falls by a substantial 4.6 percentage points when higher fines are accompanied by additional penalty points.

items.title: The Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis: Detection, Attribution, and Network-Mediated Efficiency
items.abstract: We propose the Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis (NAMH), a novel extension of the adaptive markets framework that conceptualizes market efficiency as a network-dependent equilibrium emerging from long-memory predictability and cross-market information transmission. Using G20 equity indices and five commodity futures over 2001-2026, we identify Japan as the central information hub, while the United States primarily acts as an information broadcaster. Contrary to conventional expectations, systemic crises do not exhibit higher network spectral radii, challenging the assumption that crisis-related fragility necessarily manifests through increased network amplification. Instead, crisis-related spectral contributions are dominated by Australia and the United States. Importantly, variance-decomposition connectedness is more closely associated with network modularity than with spectral radius, with crisis-period increases driven primarily by cross-cluster spillovers. Notably, efficiency-based market groupings explain network connectedness only marginally compared with geography and asset class, while the middle efficiency tier consistently exhibits the greatest idiosyncratic behaviour.

items.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
items.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras.

items.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
items.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

items.abstract: Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. items.abstract: Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge. Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation. items.title: Computer-Use Agents Are Embodied Generalists
items.abstract: In many areas of AI, general-purpose models have increasingly replaced handcrafted methods and specialized architectures. We argue that embodied AI is poised for a similar shift. Our key claim is that embodied tasks can be formulated as interaction with digital software. Specifically, we build software that renders an agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provides controls for acting in it. A computer-use agent (CUA) can then perform embodied tasks through the same screenshots and keyboard and mouse actions that it uses to operate ordinary software. Using a single CUA design and changing only the software, our entries win first-, second-, third-, and sixth-place prizes across four ECCV workshop competitions, without any competition-specific agent tuning. These results suggest that the skills CUAs learn on software, such as visual grounding, precise clicking, and exploration, already carry over to embodied tasks, giving CUAs a far broader scope in embodied AI than previously realized. items.abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.

items.title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
items.abstract: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. items.title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. items.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
items.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. items.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
items.abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. items.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power
items.abstract: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.

items.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
items.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. items.abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. items.abstract: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. items.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
items.abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. items.abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. items.abstract: External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. items.title: Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
items.abstract: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. items.title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. items.abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. items.abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

items.abstract: In the healthcare sector, claim denials impose significant financial and administrative burdens, emphasizing the need for automated and trustworthy decision-support systems. items.abstract: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. items.title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
items.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. items.abstract: Controllable molecule generation is crucial for diverse scientific applications, such as drug discovery and materials design. items.abstract: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose the activations of large language models into human-interpretable features and trace how these features interact across layers to form circuits, making them a key tool for mechanistic interpretability. items.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
items.abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. items.abstract: How does cross-border ownership shape the lithium supply chain? Using global data on mines and refineries, I estimate a model in which ownership can lower refiners' effective ore costs, encourage mines to restrict spot sales, and soften competition. items.abstract: In many choice settings, a rise in aggregate demand for an option lowers an individual's payoff from choosing it. items.abstract: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers' consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. items.abstract: A principal chooses an action using advice from an expert who privately knows local conditions. Before receiving advice, she can commission a public study of an independent state, such as future demand, that changes the expected conflict between their preferred actions. We show that the communication protocol determines the optimal study. Under optimal mediation, the value of advice is convex in conflict, making full revelation optimal. Under commitment to an action rule, the principal may prefer no information, while informative optimal studies include a report certifying high conflict. Under unmediated cheap talk, changes in the number of equilibrium messages create upward kinks in the value of advice. Optimal studies avoid interior communication thresholds and can induce two distant communication regimes while skipping every regime in between, strictly outperforming both full revelation and no information. items.abstract: Electric robotaxis are rapidly expanding from pilots to scaled commercial deployment; unlike traditional human-driven ride-hailing vehicles, they require centralized fleet control and careful management of vehicle state of charge (SoC). Each location has a battery threshold such that vehicles should return to the depot to recharge when their SoC is below it and should not do so when their SoC is above it. Vehicles should not reposition below the same threshold either; above it, the choice of destination depends on whether a vehicle's SoC matches the destination's battery sensitivity, a notion we introduce in the paper. items.abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. items.abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. items.abstract: We study the procurement of verifiable evidence from an expert who privately assesses a binary state and chooses the direction and intensity of evidence acquisition. items.abstract: Advances in technology decrease the costs of offering and choosing from large menus of varieties. items.abstract: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. items.abstract: Subgame-perfect equilibrium need not exist in continuous games with perfect information when Nature moves. items.abstract: Information designers, such as large language models and online platforms, often do not know the subjective beliefs of their receivers or users. items.abstract: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. items.abstract: We study binary choice under uncertainty when the comparison between two acts can depend on the joint distribution of their realized outcomes. This motivates correlation probabilistic sophistication (CPS), a subjective reduction principle that extends both probabilistic sophistication and Fishburn's nontransitive subjective expected utility. We show how simultaneous event exchangeability elicits a unique solvable finitely additive subjective probability and reduces binary comparisons of acts to induced joint laws. Under convex range, the induced domain coincides with the full finite joint-law domain, allowing the transfer of correlation-utility representations from risk and, under completeness and Strong Independence, correlation expected utility with a skew-symmetric comparison kernel. Under completeness and transitivity, CPS collapses to ordinary probabilistic sophistication. We further extend the framework to multiple small worlds, allowing correlation sensitivity to vary with the source of uncertainty.

items.abstract: Bankruptcy rules are rules for dividing an insufficient estate among people with different claims. Existing rules assume that the claims are publicly known. When this is not the case, claimants have a strong incentive to claim more than they are due, as bankruptcy rules give larger allocations to claimants with larger claims. A remedy often used by legal systems is to make over-reporting costly by requiring evidence and imposing penalties. items.title: Designing AI-Mediated Communication in Teams
items.abstract: AI assistants increasingly participate in work that requires employees to exchange information and coordinate decisions. We study how a firm should design this communication when workers' interests conflict with each other's and the firm's. Two workers privately know local conditions and their preferred responses, while the assistant knows aggregate project conditions. The firm discloses project information before workers report and choose their own actions. Transparency improves adaptation but can undermine truthful preference reporting. When workers agree with the firm on the productive direction, coarsening project information under weak coordination can preserve useful preference reporting at a cost in forecast precision. Under strong coordination, the firm instead prefers full project disclosure and factual reports, because preference information induces costly accommodation of private objectives. items.title: Auction Design with Private Priors and Costly Learning
items.abstract: We study two-stage auctions in which bidders privately know their valuation priors and learning costs, while the seller jointly designs information acquisition, continuation allocation, and payments. Revenue maximization requires screening learning costs while satisfying cross-prior incentives, potentially distorting both experimentation and continuation allocation. We derive a revenue representation involving allocated posterior values, virtual learning costs, and prior-dependent rents, and characterize cross-prior incentives through difference inequalities. We establish existence of optimal mechanisms for finite experiment menus and arbitrary prior distributions. With finite prior support, bounded finite-category linear programs approximate optimal revenue at a linear rate while preserving exact dynamic incentive compatibility and interim individual rationality. Their dual yields joint optimality conditions for experimentation, allocation, and payments. A two-prior example demonstrates that efficient continuation can be revenue-suboptimal and that cost-contingent experimentation can strictly increase revenue.

items.title: Agreements Have a Clock: Compute Growth and the Verification of AI Restraint
items.abstract: Rival powers have agreed to limit nuclear arms, phase out ozone-depleting chemicals, and cut greenhouse gases, though each agreement was hard to reach. This paper asks what an agreement to pause frontier AI needs. A follower advances through own research and diffusion from the leader. Because diffusion fades as the gap closes, a paused leader stays ahead longer than its raw lead suggests. A solved agreement game adds voluntary entry, costly monitoring, secret advances, and credible responses. Cooperation is supportable when the monitoring needed to deter a breakout costs no more than either country gains from cooperating. As compute grows during a pause, a secret advance reaches the frozen frontier sooner, shrinking the response window: agreements have a clock. In an example with a fixed leader window, cooperation is supportable through month 18.9. Verified matched safety research extends this to month 25.5, and halving the monitoring cost to month 31.8.

items.title: Prizes, Shared Hazard, and the Speed of Frontier AI
items.abstract: Frontier AI labs compete in a contest for commercial leadership while sharing the risk of catastrophe. Each lab gains from arriving earlier but bears only part of the hazard its speed adds, which this paper calls the hazard externality. In an illustrative calibrated takeoff model, three racing labs get through the takeoff period in 18 months, while a common rule on research shares would stretch it to 69 months. Neither force alone explains racing that fast. Removing the contest first closes over ninety percent of the gap in catastrophe probability between racing and a common rule when the catastrophe probability at full speed is 75 percent, and 69 percent when it is 25 percent; averaged over both orders of removal, the contest explains 65 and 44 percent. More labs make each lab race harder, when industry hazard at a common research share does not depend on the number of labs. items.title: Optimal Subsidy Design for Productive Investment across Markets
items.abstract: We study the optimal design of investment subsidies across heterogeneous monopolistic markets subject to a common expected discounted budget. Each producer faces a regular one-dimensional demand diffusion and chooses irreversible capacity expansion through a singular stochastic control problem. The regulator values weighted consumer surplus, producer profits, and an additional benefit from installed capacity, while accounting for the excess cost of raising public funds. We characterize producers' optimal investment responses through free boundaries and reformulate the regulator's stochastic optimization problem as a deterministic optimization over investment boundaries. An integral representation then recovers the optimal subsidy schedules that implement the resulting capacity policies. Under mild conditions on the diffusions, we establish existence of optimal schedules and uniqueness of the induced investment policies. Finally, we characterize the subsidy schedule and provide numerical illustrations.
